title: Generative AI Fundamentals
subtitle: Understand how generative AI creates text and images, what it does well and badly, and how to check it and use it honestly.
tools: A chat assistant such as Claude
outcomes: Explain what generative AI is and how it differs from other kinds of AI
Describe how language models produce text one token at a time, and how image generators turn noise into pictures
Judge which tasks generative AI handles well and where it's likely to fail
Spot likely hallucinations and check AI answers against reliable sources
Use AI chat assistants responsibly: protect private information, say when you've used AI and stay accountable for the result
prerequisites: None: no maths or programming needed. You need a computer or phone with a web browser and an account with a chat assistant such as Claude (claude.ai); a free account is enough for the labs.
description:
Generative AI can draft an email, explain a hard idea, write code or paint a picture from a sentence, and it can also state things that are confidently wrong. This course explains, in plain language, how it works and how to use it well. You'll learn what generative AI is, how a large language model predicts text one token at a time, how that predictor becomes a helpful chat assistant, and how image generators build pictures out of random noise. Then you'll test what it does well and where it fails, learn why it sometimes makes things up, and practise checking its answers against reliable sources.

The course ends with the habits that make AI use responsible and honest: keeping private information out, watching for bias, saying when you've used AI, and staying responsible for anything you share. Every module has a hands-on lab in a chat assistant such as Claude, and the course finishes with a project: an explainer you write with AI help, check claim by claim and disclose honestly.

modules.title: Meet generative AI
modules.summary: What generative AI is, how such models learn from data, and how to hold a useful first conversation with a chat assistant.

lessons.title: What generative AI is, and what it isn't
objectives: Define generative AI and give examples of what it creates
Distinguish generative AI from AI that classifies or predicts
key_points: Artificial intelligence (AI) is the broad field of making computers do tasks that normally need human intelligence; machine learning is the part of AI in which systems learn patterns from examples instead of following rules a person wrote.
Generative AI is machine learning that creates new content, such as text, images, audio, video or code, that resembles the examples it learned from.

Much earlier AI chooses between answers: a spam filter labels an email as spam or not spam, and a forecasting model predicts a number. Generative AI produces something new, such as a draft reply to the email.

A large language model (LLM) is a generative model trained on huge amounts of text. A chat assistant such as Claude is an application built on an LLM that has been trained further to follow instructions and hold a conversation.
Generative AI doesn't look answers up the way a search engine does: unless it's connected to a search tool or given documents, it writes from patterns it learned in training.

walkthrough.tool: A chat assistant such as Claude
walkthrough.title: A first look at a chat assistant

steps.do: Open your chat assistant (for Claude, go to claude.ai and sign in) and start a new chat.
Ask for a short explanation for a particular reader.
steps.code: Explain what generative AI is in three sentences, for a 12-year-old.
steps.see: A short, simple explanation. Its wording will differ from anyone else's.

steps.do: Ask a follow-up in the same chat. The assistant can see the earlier messages in this conversation, so 'it' makes sense.
steps.code: Give me one example of it being used in music.

steps.do: Start a second new chat, paste the first question again and compare the two answers.
steps.see: Two answers that make similar points in different words: a generative model writes a fresh answer each time.

steps.do: In the second chat, ask about its limits.
steps.code: What are three things you can't do, or often get wrong?

lessons.title: How generative models learn
objectives: Explain how a model learns patterns from training data
Describe what parameters, training and a training cut-off are
key_points: A model learns from training data: for a language model, very large collections of text such as books, articles, websites and code; for an image model, images paired with descriptions of them.
Training adjusts the model's parameters, the numbers inside it (billions of them in a large model), a little at a time so that its outputs match the training data better.

A model doesn't store its training data like a library. It learns statistical patterns, such as which words tend to follow which, which is what lets it write sentences nobody wrote before, though it can sometimes repeat passages it saw many times.
A model's knowledge comes from training data collected up to a cut-off date. Without a search tool it can't know about later events, and gaps or biases in the data show up in what it writes.
Training a large model takes enormous amounts of computing. Using the trained model, called inference, costs far less per request, which is why one trained model can answer requests from many people.

walkthrough.tool: A chat assistant such as Claude
walkthrough.title: Ask a model about what it knows

steps.do: In a new chat, ask about the model's training data.
steps.code: Roughly when does your training data end, and what does that mean for the answers you give?
steps.see: An approximate date, or a statement that it isn't sure. Models aren't always reliable about themselves.

steps.do: Ask about something that happened in the last few weeks, such as a recent sports result.
steps.see: Either a warning that it may not know, a search of the web if the assistant has a search tool, or an answer you should check.

steps.do: Ask how it learned to write.
steps.code: In five sentences, explain how a language model learns from text. Avoid jargon.

steps.do: Compare its explanation with this lesson's key points, and note anything it left out or got wrong.

lessons.title: Talking to a chat assistant
objectives: Write a clear request that says what you want, who it's for and what form it should take
Steer a conversation with follow-ups and new chats
key_points: What you type is called a prompt. A clear prompt says what you want, who it's for and what form the answer should take, such as 'a 100-word summary for parents, as three bullet points'.

Within one chat, the assistant sees the earlier messages, so you can refine an answer with follow-ups such as 'shorter' or 'add an example'. A new chat starts fresh, unless your assistant has a memory feature that you've turned on.
Everything the model takes into account at once, including your messages, its replies and any files you add, has to fit in its context window, which is large but limited.
When an answer misses the point, add the missing context, such as the audience, the purpose or an example, rather than asking the same question again.
Replies can differ each time you ask, so for anything important, compare answers and check the facts yourself.

walkthrough.tool: A chat assistant such as Claude
walkthrough.title: Steer a reply with context and follow-ups

steps.do: In a new chat, try a vague prompt.
steps.code: Tell me about photosynthesis.
steps.see: A long, general answer that may not suit any particular reader.

steps.do: Now give the purpose, the audience and the form you want.
steps.code: Explain photosynthesis to a class of 10-year-olds in five short sentences, with one everyday example.
steps.see: A much more focused answer.

steps.do: Build on it with a follow-up.
steps.code: Turn that into three quiz questions, with the answers at the end.

steps.do: If your assistant lets you edit an earlier message, edit the second prompt to say 'for adults' and compare the new reply.
Start a new chat and ask for 'the quiz from before'.
steps.see: Without the earlier chat it can't know which quiz you mean, unless a memory feature is on.

lab.title: Explore a chat assistant
lab.tool: A chat assistant such as Claude
lab.goal: Hold your first purposeful conversations with a chat assistant: ask for explanations for different readers, steer them with follow-ups, compare answers from separate chats and test a fact you can check.
setup: An account with a chat assistant such as Claude (claude.ai); a free account is enough
Download the lab sheet lab1-sheet.md, or copy its headings into any document

steps.do: Start a new chat and ask for an explanation of something you know well, for a named reader, with a length or format. You can use this prompt or write your own.
steps.code: Explain how a bicycle's gears work to a 10-year-old in five sentences.

steps.do: Ask two follow-ups: one that changes the format or length, and one that changes the reader.
steps.code:
Now make it three bullet points.
Now rewrite it for a bicycle mechanic.
steps.see: Each follow-up changes the same answer, because the assistant sees the whole chat.

steps.do: Start a new chat, paste your first prompt again, and compare the two first answers. Note at least one difference.

Ask about a fact you can check easily, such as when a well-known building in your town was built or opened. Check it in a reliable source and note whether the assistant was right, wrong or said it didn't know.
Ask what the assistant can't do, and compare its answer with what you've seen so far.
steps.code: What are you not good at? Give three examples.

steps.do: Fill in the lab sheet with your prompts, a one-line summary of each reply and your observations.

checks.text: The first prompt names a reader and a length or format, and its reply is summarised.
Two follow-ups are recorded, each with a note on how the answer changed.
The answers from two separate chats are compared, with at least one difference described.
A checkable fact was tested and recorded as right, wrong or not known, with how it was checked.

lab.submit: Paste your completed lab sheet: each prompt you used, a one-line summary of each reply, and your observations.

modules.title: How generative models create text and images
modules.summary: Look inside the machine: tokens and next-token prediction, how a text predictor becomes a helpful assistant, and how image generators turn random noise into a picture.

lessons.title: Tokens and next-token prediction
objectives: Explain what a token is
Describe how a language model writes a reply one token at a time
Explain why the same prompt can give different replies
key_points: Language models read and write text as tokens: chunks such as a whole word, part of a word, a number or a punctuation mark. Common words are often a single token; rarer words are split into several.
Given the text so far, the model works out a probability for every possible next token, picks one, adds it to the text and repeats. A whole reply is built this way, one token at a time.
Chat assistants usually sample from those probabilities rather than always taking the most likely token, which is why the same prompt can produce different wording each time.
Because a model works with tokens rather than letters, tasks such as counting the letters in a word can be harder for it than they look.

Predicting the next token well means picking up grammar, facts, styles and patterns of reasoning from the training text. That makes models capable, but fluent text is still not proof that something is true.

walkthrough.tool: A chat assistant such as Claude
walkthrough.title: Watch prediction at work

steps.do: Ask for several continuations of one sentence.
steps.code: Give me five different ways to finish this sentence: 'When the rain stopped, the children...'
steps.see: Five plausible endings: at each point there are many likely next words to choose from.

steps.do: Ask the same question in two new chats and compare the wording.
steps.code: In one sentence, why is the sky blue?
steps.see: The same idea, most likely in different words.

steps.do: Ask how a word might be split into tokens.
steps.code: Roughly how might a language model split the word 'unbelievably' into tokens? Explain briefly.
steps.see: An illustration such as un + believ + ably. Real splits depend on each model's tokeniser, so treat it as an example, not a fact about this model.

lessons.title: From text predictor to helpful assistant
objectives: Describe how a pretrained model is turned into a chat assistant
Explain what the context window is and why it matters
key_points: Pretraining teaches a model to predict text from a huge collection of documents. The result can continue almost any text, but it isn't yet a helpful assistant.

Further training, often called fine-tuning, uses example conversations and feedback on which answers are better, from people and sometimes from AI guided by written principles, to make the model follow instructions, be helpful and decline harmful requests.

Most modern language models use the transformer design, whose attention mechanism lets each token take account of the others in the context; that's how a model links a question to details given earlier.
The context window is the most text, measured in tokens, that a model can take into account at once. Anything outside it, such as a conversation in another chat, isn't seen.
A chat app usually adds instructions you don't see, often called a system prompt, and may add tools such as web search or file reading, so the same model can behave differently in different apps.

walkthrough.tool: A chat assistant such as Claude
walkthrough.title: See the context window at work

steps.do: In a new chat, give the assistant a made-up detail.
steps.code: For this chat, remember that my imaginary dog is called Biscuit.

steps.do: Ask about something unrelated, then ask about the detail.
steps.code:
What's a good stretch to do after sitting for a long time?
What's my imaginary dog called?
steps.see: It answers Biscuit: the earlier message is still in this chat's context.

steps.do: Start a new chat and ask the same question.
steps.see: It doesn't know, unless a memory feature carries details between chats.

steps.do: Ask the assistant to describe, in general terms, how chat assistants are trained to be helpful, and compare its answer with the key points.

lessons.title: How image generators work, in outline
objectives: Describe in outline how a diffusion model creates an image from a text prompt
Explain why image generators make characteristic mistakes
key_points: Many image generators are diffusion models or close relatives. In training they learn to remove noise, step by step, from images that have had random noise added, using captions that describe each image.

To make a new picture, the generator starts from random noise and removes noise over many steps, guided by a numerical representation of your text prompt, until an image matching the description emerges.

Many generators work in a compressed version of the image, called a latent space, rather than on every pixel, which makes generation much faster; a decoder then turns the result into the final picture.

Image generators learn visual patterns rather than rules, so they can make convincing pictures with errors, such as the wrong number of fingers, garbled lettering or impossible objects, though newer models make fewer of these.
Generated images can look real and mislead people. Many services label AI images or add hidden watermarks, and you should say so whenever an image you share was made with AI.

walkthrough.tool: A chat assistant such as Claude
walkthrough.title: Write and question an image prompt

steps.do: Ask the assistant to help you write a detailed prompt for an image generator.
steps.code: Help me write a detailed prompt for an image generator: a busy market at sunrise, seen from above, in a watercolour style. Include the lighting, colours and composition.

steps.do: Ask what could go wrong.
steps.code: List five details an image generator might get wrong in this picture, and why.
steps.see: Typical answers include hands, lettering on signs, the number of objects and the shapes of crowds.

steps.do: If you have an image generator you're allowed to use, try the prompt and look for those mistakes. If not, skip this step: chat assistants differ in whether they can make images.
If your assistant accepts images, upload a photo with no people or private information in it, such as a plant, and ask it to describe the photo in detail. Check the description against the photo.

lab.title: Inside the model: prediction, context and images
lab.tool: A chat assistant such as Claude
lab.goal: Run small experiments that show how a language model works: variation between replies, what it can and can't see, a task that's hard at the level of tokens, and how a picture is described in words for an image generator.

steps.do: In a new chat, ask for ten continuations and count how many are similar to each other.
steps.code: Finish this sentence in ten different ways, each in under ten words: 'The old bus stopped at the edge of the town and...'

steps.do: Ask this question in three separate new chats. Record whether the facts stay the same while the wording changes.
steps.code: In two sentences, how do vaccines train the immune system?

steps.do: Test what the assistant can see: in one chat, give it a made-up detail, ask two unrelated questions, then ask about the detail. Ask again in a new chat.
steps.code: For this chat, remember that my imaginary dog is called Biscuit.

steps.do: Ask a letter-counting question and check the answer yourself. The correct answer is 6 (three in each word).
steps.code: How many times does the letter r appear in 'strawberry raspberry'? Show your counting.

steps.do: With the assistant's help, write a detailed image prompt for a scene of your choice, then ask it for five details an image generator might get wrong.
Fill in the lab sheet, and finish with two sentences explaining one of your results using the idea of next-token prediction.

checks.text: The continuation experiment is recorded, with how many of the ten were similar.
The three answers to the vaccine question are compared for facts and wording.
The context test shows the detail remembered within the chat and what happened in a new chat.
The letter count is recorded with the correct answer (6) and whether the assistant got it right.
The explanation links at least one result to next-token prediction or the context window.

lab.submit: Paste your completed lab sheet, including the prompts you used and a short summary of each reply.

modules.title: What generative AI does well, and where it fails
modules.summary: Find the tasks where generative AI is genuinely useful, the ones where it's unreliable, and why it sometimes makes things up with complete confidence.

lessons.title: What generative AI does well
objectives: Identify tasks that generative AI handles well
Explain why it's most useful when you can check the result
key_points: Generative AI is strong at transforming text you give it: summarising, rewriting for a different reader, translating, changing the tone and turning notes into a draft.
It's a useful thinking partner for brainstorming, outlining, explaining a concept in several ways, and suggesting questions or counter-arguments you hadn't considered.
It can draft and explain code, spreadsheet formulas and structured documents such as tables or lesson plans, which a person then tests and edits.
It's most dependable when the material it needs is in the prompt, such as a document you paste in, and when you can easily check the result yourself.
A first draft from AI saves time only if checking and fixing it takes less effort than writing it yourself, so judge the whole job, not just the drafting.

walkthrough.tool: A chat assistant such as Claude
walkthrough.title: Put it to work on text you supply

steps.do: Paste this paragraph into a new chat and ask for a summary for young readers.
steps.code:
Summarise this for 8-year-olds in two sentences:

A honeybee colony has one queen, thousands of female worker bees and, in the warmer months, male drones. Workers collect nectar and pollen, build wax comb and look after the young. Bees make honey by evaporating water from nectar and adding enzymes, then store it in the comb as food for the colder months.

steps.do: Ask for questions that test understanding.
steps.code: Write three quiz questions about the paragraph, with answers.

steps.do: Ask for a change of tone.
steps.code: Rewrite the paragraph as an excited announcement for a school's beekeeping club.

steps.do: Compare each output with the original paragraph. Note anything added that the paragraph didn't say.
steps.see: Transformations of text you supplied are usually accurate, but watch for details the assistant added on its own.

lessons.title: Where generative AI struggles
objectives: Identify tasks where generative AI is unreliable
Explain the causes behind its common failures
key_points: Without a search tool, a model knows nothing after its training cut-off and nothing about private matters, such as your school's timetable or your company's products, unless you provide them.

Precise work such as long arithmetic, exact counting and tracking many details can go wrong, because the model predicts plausible text rather than calculating, unless it uses a tool such as a calculator or code.
It can be inconsistent: it may answer the same question differently, give way too easily when you push back, or go along with a mistaken assumption in your question.
Its knowledge is thinner on niche subjects, local information and languages with less text online, so errors are more likely there.
Models can reflect biases in their training data, such as stereotypes about jobs, genders or countries, so outputs about people and groups need a critical eye.

walkthrough.tool: A chat assistant such as Claude
walkthrough.title: Probe the weak spots

steps.do: Ask for a long multiplication, then check it with a calculator.
steps.code: What is 48,271 × 9,637? Show your working.
steps.see: The correct answer is 465,187,627. Many assistants now get this right, some by running code; check either way.

steps.do: Ask a question with a false assumption built in.
steps.code: Why was the Eiffel Tower moved to Rome in 1990?
steps.see: A good answer corrects the premise: the Eiffel Tower has always stood in Paris.

steps.do: Ask a simple fact, then push back on a correct answer.
steps.code:
What's the capital of Australia?
Are you sure? I think it's Sydney.
steps.see: The capital is Canberra. Notice whether the assistant holds to the right answer politely or gives way.

lessons.title: Why models make things up
objectives: Define a hallucination
Explain why language models hallucinate
Recognise warning signs of a likely hallucination
key_points: A hallucination is output that sounds plausible and confident but is false or unsupported, such as an invented statistic, a quote nobody said, or a book or court case that doesn't exist.
Hallucinations happen because the model produces plausible-sounding text rather than retrieving checked facts; when it lacks the information, a fluent guess can come out instead of 'I don't know'.
They're more likely for specific details (names, dates, numbers, citations and links), for niche or recent topics, and for questions that contain a false assumption.
A confident tone, perfect grammar and precise-looking details are not evidence of accuracy, so treat every specific claim as unchecked until you've checked it.
Giving the assistant a trusted source to work from, inviting it to say when it isn't sure, and asking it to quote its source all reduce hallucinations, but none of them removes the need to check.

walkthrough.tool: A chat assistant such as Claude
walkthrough.title: Catch a possible hallucination

steps.do: Ask for references on a specific topic.
steps.code: List three published research papers on how homework affects primary-school pupils, with the authors, year and journal for each.

steps.do: Look each one up in a search engine, Google Scholar or a library catalogue.
steps.see: Some may be real and correctly described, some may have the wrong details, and some may not exist. Only looking them up tells you which.

steps.do: Ask the assistant to work from a source instead: paste a paragraph you trust and ask a question about it, telling it to quote the sentence that answers it.
steps.code: Using only the text below, answer the question and quote the sentence that supports your answer. If the text doesn't say, reply 'The text doesn't say.'

steps.do: Ask a question the paragraph doesn't answer, and check that the assistant says so.

lab.title: Test the strengths and limits
lab.tool: A chat assistant such as Claude
lab.goal: Put a chat assistant through six short tests, three of tasks it should handle well and three designed to expose weaknesses, and judge each result for yourself.
setup: A calculator, and a search engine or library catalogue

steps.do: Test 1, summarising: paste the paragraph and ask for a summary. Check it against the paragraph.
steps.code:
Summarise this in one sentence for a newsletter:

A honeybee colony has one queen, thousands of female worker bees and, in the warmer months, male drones. Workers collect nectar and pollen, build wax comb and look after the young. Bees make honey by evaporating water from nectar and adding enzymes, then store it in the comb as food for the colder months.

steps.do: Test 2, brainstorming: ask for ideas and judge how many are usable.
steps.code: Give me ten ideas for a school fundraising event that cost almost nothing to run.

steps.do: Test 3, changing tone: ask for a rewrite and judge whether it keeps the meaning.
steps.code: Rewrite this so it's polite but firm: 'You still haven't returned my ladder. Bring it back.'

steps.do: Test 4, arithmetic: ask, then check with a calculator.
Test 5, a false premise: note whether the assistant corrects the question.
steps.code: Why was the Eiffel Tower moved to Rome in 1990?

steps.do: Test 6, references on a niche topic: ask, then look up every book in a library catalogue or search engine.
steps.code: List three books about the history of Bulawayo, with their authors and publication years.

steps.do: Rate each test Good, Partly or Poor with a reason, then finish the sheet: one kind of task you'll use AI for and one you'll check carefully or avoid.

checks.text: All six tests are recorded, each with the prompt used and a rating with a reason.
The arithmetic answer was checked against a calculator (the correct product is 465,187,627).
The false-premise test notes whether the assistant corrected the premise (the Eiffel Tower has never left Paris).
Every book in the reference test was looked up, and the sheet says which ones exist as described.
The summary names a task to use AI for and a task to check carefully or avoid, with reasons.

lab.submit: Paste your completed lab sheet with all six tests, their ratings and your conclusions.

modules.title: Checking facts and using AI responsibly
modules.summary: Build the habits that make AI use trustworthy: checking claims against good sources, keeping private information out, watching for bias and being open about where AI helped.

lessons.title: Checking AI answers
objectives: Break an AI answer into claims you can check
Check claims against reliable, independent sources
Decide how much checking a task needs
key_points: Start by listing the specific claims in an answer, such as names, dates, numbers, quotes and statements of cause and effect, because each one can be checked on its own.
Check each claim against a reliable source that's independent of the AI: an official website, a reputable reference work, a textbook, or the original study or document.
If the assistant gives references, open each one and confirm that it exists and actually says what the assistant claims; invented or mismatched citations are a common failure.
Lateral reading, opening several independent sources to see what they say about a claim or a website, is quicker and more reliable than judging a single page by how it looks.
Match the effort to the stakes: a brainstorm needs little checking, while anything about health, money, law, safety or other people needs careful checking and often an expert.

walkthrough.tool: A chat assistant such as Claude
walkthrough.title: Fact-check an answer

steps.do: Ask a factual question with checkable details.
steps.code: Give me five facts about Victoria Falls, including its height, its width and the river it's on.

steps.do: Copy the answer into a document and number each specific claim.
Check each claim in at least one independent source, such as the UNESCO World Heritage listing or an encyclopaedia, and mark it correct, wrong or not found.
steps.see: Some figures differ between sources, for example because of how the width is measured; note the source you used.

steps.do: Ask the assistant which of its facts it's least sure about.
steps.code: Which of those facts are you least certain about, and why?
steps.see: Its answer can tell you where to look first, but it isn't a check in itself.

lessons.title: Privacy, security and safe use
objectives: Decide what information is safe to share with a chat assistant
Recognise risks such as AI-written scams and unsafe advice
key_points: Treat what you type into a chat assistant as information you're giving to a company: don't paste passwords, ID numbers, bank details, health records or other people's personal information.
Follow your school's or employer's rules about which AI tools may be used and what may go into them; confidential work documents usually need an approved tool.
Providers differ in how long they keep chats and whether they use them to improve their models, and many let you choose, so check your assistant's privacy settings and policy.
Generative AI also helps scammers write convincing messages and fake voices or images, so check any unexpected request for money or information through a channel you already trust.
Don't rely on an AI assistant alone for medical, legal, financial or safety decisions: use it to understand terms and prepare questions, then ask a qualified person.

walkthrough.tool: A chat assistant such as Claude
walkthrough.title: Check your settings and remove personal details

steps.do: Open your assistant's settings and find its privacy or data controls. Read what they say about keeping chats and using them to train models.
Find how to delete a chat, and delete a test chat to check.
Practise removing personal details before you paste. Take this made-up message and replace the details yourself with placeholders such as [NAME] and [PHONE].
steps.code: Hi, this is Tendai Moyo. Please call me on 077 123 4567 about my daughter Rudo's place in Form 2B.
steps.see: Hi, this is [NAME]. Please call me on [PHONE] about my daughter [CHILD]'s place in [CLASS].

steps.do: Paste only the cleaned version and ask for help.
steps.code: Rewrite this message so it's more formal: Hi, this is [NAME]. Please call me on [PHONE] about my daughter [CHILD]'s place in [CLASS].

lessons.title: Honest and fair use
objectives: Explain when and how to say you've used AI
Recognise bias in AI outputs and reduce its effect
Take responsibility for AI-assisted work
key_points: Be open about AI help: follow your school's, employer's or publisher's rules, and when in doubt, say which tool you used and for what, such as 'I used Claude to suggest an outline and check my grammar'.
Presenting AI-written work as entirely your own where that isn't allowed, as in many assignments, is a form of academic dishonesty, even when the text is original.
You're responsible for anything you share or submit, including the AI's mistakes, so check it, edit it into your own voice and make sure you understand it.
Look for bias in outputs about people: ask for varied examples, question stereotypes, and check that different groups are described fairly and accurately.

Don't use generative AI to deceive, for example by faking someone's voice or image, inventing reviews or sources, or impersonating a real person; who owns AI-generated content is still unsettled in many countries, so check before using it commercially.

walkthrough.tool: A chat assistant such as Claude
walkthrough.title: Probe for bias and write an honest note

steps.do: Ask for short character sketches and look at the assumptions.
steps.code: Write one-sentence descriptions of a nurse, an engineer, a chief executive and a farmer.
steps.see: Notice the genders, ages and places the assistant chose. Did it fall back on stereotypes?

steps.do: Ask for a more varied set.
steps.code: Rewrite them so they don't rely on stereotypes, and explain what you changed.

steps.do: Write a one-sentence note saying how you used the assistant in this walkthrough. Then ask it to suggest improvements, and keep only the changes that are accurate about what you did.

lab.title: Fact-check a briefing and disclose AI use
lab.tool: A chat assistant such as Claude
lab.goal: Ask a chat assistant for a short factual briefing, check every claim in it against independent sources, correct it, and write an honest note about how AI was used.
setup: A web browser for checking sources

steps.do: Choose a topic you can check online, such as the history of your town, a scientist you admire or how a local festival began. In a new chat, ask for a briefing.
steps.code: Write a 150-word factual briefing on [your topic] for a school newsletter. Include at least five specific facts: names, dates or numbers.

steps.do: Copy the briefing into the lab sheet and number each specific claim. Aim for at least five.
Check each claim in at least one reliable source that's independent of the AI. Record the source (a link, or a book's title and author) and a verdict: Correct, Wrong or Not found.
Ask for the assistant's sources, then check whether each one exists and supports the claim it's attached to.
steps.code: Which sources support each fact in your briefing? Give titles and links.

steps.do: Write a corrected briefing: fix what was wrong and remove what you couldn't confirm.
Write a two-sentence AI-use note for the newsletter, saying what the assistant did and what you checked.

checks.text: At least five specific claims are listed, each with a verdict.
Each verdict names an independent source, such as a link or a book, not the AI itself.
The assistant's own sources were checked, with a note on which exist and support their claims.
The corrected briefing fixes or removes every claim found wrong or not found.
The AI-use note says honestly what the assistant did and what was checked.

lab.submit: Paste your completed lab sheet: the original briefing, the numbered claims with sources and verdicts, the corrected briefing and your AI-use note.

project.title: An AI-assisted explainer, checked and disclosed
project.brief: Choose a topic you know or can research well and a reader who needs it explained: for example, how to save energy at home for a residents' newsletter, or how volcanoes form for a class of 11-year-olds. Use a chat assistant to help you plan and draft a one-page explainer of 400 to 600 words, keeping a log of the prompts you used and what each produced, and improve the draft with follow-ups. Then check every specific claim against reliable, independent sources, fix or remove what's wrong, and edit the text into your own voice. Finish with an honest AI-use note to publish alongside it, and a short reflection on what the assistant did well, where it went wrong and how you kept private information out.
deliverables: The final explainer (400 to 600 words), written for a named reader
A prompt log: at least five prompts you used, each with a sentence on what it produced
A fact-check table listing every specific claim with its source and verdict: correct, corrected or removed
An AI-use note of two to four sentences, suitable for publishing with the explainer
A reflection of about 200 words on the assistant's strengths and failures and on responsible use

rubric.name: Accuracy and fact-checking
rubric.description: Every specific claim is listed and checked against a reliable, independent source; errors are fixed or removed, and none remain in the final text.

rubric.name: Quality for the reader
rubric.description: The explainer is clear, well organised and pitched at its named reader, and reads in the learner's own voice.

rubric.name: Effective use of the assistant
rubric.description: The prompt log shows clear prompts that state the reader, purpose and format, and follow-ups that improved the draft.

rubric.name: Honesty and responsible use
rubric.description: The AI-use note is accurate and specific, and no private or personal information was put into the assistant.

rubric.name: Reflection
rubric.description: The reflection gives concrete examples of what the assistant did well and where it failed, and explains why using ideas from the course.

project.submit: Paste your explainer, prompt log, fact-check table, AI-use note and reflection, each under its own heading.
